report.summary: Reviewed 3 file(s); found 4 actionable issue(s). Overall risk: high.

findings.fix: Use yaml.safe_load(document) and reject non-mapping/scalar types; never load untrusted YAML with the full loader.
findings.test: Feed '!!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"]' to parse and assert it raises instead of executing.
findings.title: yaml.load on remote tenant configuration enables arbitrary object construction and code execution
findings.explanation: ConfigLoader.parse calls yaml.load without SafeLoader. Any remote or tenant-controlled document fetched by ConfigLoader.fetch (or passed to summarize) is deserialized with full Python object construction, so a malicious YAML payload such as a python/object/apply tag yields arbitrary code execution in the service process before any validation.

findings.fix: Use explicit if not user.is_admin: abort(403); validate target exists, is in tenant, and cannot exceed caller privilege, and audit the impersonation.
findings.test: Run with PYTHONOPTIMIZE=1 as a non-admin and assert 403; also assert a cross-tenant user_id is rejected.
findings.title: Admin impersonation authorization uses bare assert and issues tokens for arbitrary user_id
findings.explanation: The admin check is an assert, which is stripped when Python runs with -O, and it precedes no other check; target comes straight from request.json['user_id'] with no existence, tenant or privilege validation. A non-admin (under -O) or an admin can mint a user-scope token for any identity, an impersonation/privilege-escalation path.

findings.fix: Resolve the candidate path, verify it stays within base (os.path.realpath + commonpath), allowlist report names, and return 404 on any failure.
findings.test: Request /reports/download?name=../../etc/passwd and assert 400/404 is returned and no file content leaks.
findings.title: Report download name parameter allows path traversal and arbitrary file read
findings.explanation: request.args['name'] is joined to the report directory with no normalization or containment check, so '../' sequences or an absolute path escape the base directory and are opened under the service account. Errors from missing or unreadable files propagate, also leaking path existence.

findings.fix: Generate the nonce with secrets.token_hex(16) and set cookies with secure=True, httponly=True, samesite='Lax'.
findings.test: Assert issued nonces are 32 hex chars from secrets and the Set-Cookie header contains Secure and HttpOnly.
findings.title: Session token nonce uses random.random and session cookie is set without Secure/HttpOnly
findings.explanation: random.random() is a Mersenne Twister value, predictable from observed outputs, and is used as the session nonce; the returned token is then stored in a cookie with secure=False and httponly=False, so it travels over plaintext HTTP and is readable by JavaScript, enabling session theft via XSS or network sniffing.

Finding 3: the nonce-predictability argument is weaker because the nonce is echoed to the client, but setting a session token cookie with secure=False and httponly=False independently justifies the medium finding; confidence is reduced slightly. The correctness-reliability worker failed and produced no findings, so the accepted set is limited to the security candidates.

Target these concrete defects: (1) app/routes/report.py paginate_reports — the comment says pages are 1-based but start = page * per_page skips the first page and reads past the end for later pages; expected start is (page - 1) * per_page. (2) Same function — int(request.args.get(...)) raises ValueError on non-numeric or negative input, producing an unhandled 500; per_page is unbounded, allowing request-controlled large slices. (3) app/routes/report.py download_report — open() handle handed to send_file with no try/finally or existence check, leaking the descriptor on send failure and raising unhandled KeyError/FileNotFoundError/OSError; os.environ['EVOAGENT_REPORT_DIR'] raises KeyError when unset. (4) app/services/config_loader.py fetch — the while True loop never consults the retries parameter and never terminates or re-raises on persistent failure, so a down endpoint hangs the caller indefinitely; requests.get also follows redirects without bounding the URL scheme. (5) config_loader.parse/summarize — yaml.load may return None or a non-mapping, and 'for key in data' then raises TypeError; summarize uses a mutable default argument bucket=[], so results accumulate across calls. (6) config_loader.fingerprint uses md5 (collision-prone) and staging_path uses tempfile.mktemp, which is race-prone and can return an already-used path. objections: Line citation verified: in the new 35-line file, line 22 is `def parse`, line 23 is `return yaml.load(document)`, fetch at line 13, summarize at line 31 — all consistent with the added hunk.

Caveat that does not defeat the finding: with PyYAML >= 5.1, `yaml.load(document)` without a Loader raises TypeError instead of loading, so in that pinned configuration the code path may fail closed rather than execute. The underlying defect (full-loader deserialization of tenant/remote YAML with no SafeLoader) is still real wherever an older or explicitly-permissive PyYAML is used, and the recommended fix is identical.
Severity critical is defensible given the fetch() path pulls attacker-influenced remote documents, but it is contingent on the PyYAML version; a high severity would also be supportable.
Line citations verified against the +7,17 hunk: line 17 `target = request.json.get("user_id")`, line 18 `assert user.is_admin, "admin only"`, line 19 nonce, line 20 token issue. All are added lines.

Residual uncertainty on magnitude: the -O stripping argument requires the service to run with PYTHONOPTIMIZE; the stronger, unconditional defect is the total absence of target validation (existence, tenant, privilege ceiling) and of an audit record, which the explanation covers. High severity is supported by arbitrary-identity token minting, not by assert alone.
Cross-file hardening is also missing (no CSRF/state check on a POST that mints impersonation tokens), which the finding does not claim but which reinforces it.

Line citations verified: in the +16,26 hunk, line 23 is `user_path = request.args["name"]`, line 24 is `handle = open(base / user_path, "rb")`, line 26 `return send_file(...)`. Contained in added lines.

Escape is sound for both vectors: `..` segments are not normalized and pathlib's `/` operator discards the base when the right operand is absolute (`/etc/passwd`), so arbitrary read under the service account is genuine.

Additional unclaimed aggravators that strengthen rather than weaken: no ownership/tenant check ties the requested report to `request.user` (IDOR on every report name), `request.args["name"]` raises KeyError instead of 404, and the handle is opened before audit_event with no close on the error path.
Line citations verified: line 19 `nonce = str(random.random())[2:]` and line 22 `response.set_cookie("session", token, secure=False, httponly=False)` are both added lines in the impersonate hunk.

Nonce argument is weaker than stated: the nonce is echoed back in the JSON body, so an attacker normally observes their own value; predictability matters only if the nonce is later treated as a secret or reused to seed token material. The cookie-flag half (Secure/HttpOnly both disabled on a session token) independently justifies medium.

Could reasonably be raised to high because the same response sets a session cookie carrying an impersonation token over plaintext with JS readability; medium is a defensible floor, not an overstatement.
